title: How NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS Maximizes AI Factory Throughput and Efficiency | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: A joint NVIDIA-Nscale test of DSX MaxLPS dynamic power sharing on GB300 NVL72 in Iceland ran 192 GPUs instead of 140 under the same 264.4 kW budget, lifting aggregate throughput and tokens per provisioned watt by 49.2% (4.10 to 6.12 tokens/s/W). The catch: P99 time to first token rose 17%, and the gain depends on workload mix and reliable telemetry.

themes.theme: Stranded power as hidden AI capacity

insights.claim: AI factories are typically provisioned so every GPU can hit peak power simultaneously, a rare event, leaving a protective buffer that keeps valuable infrastructure underused in normal operation.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Power, not chips, is the binding constraint; software that unlocks stranded power is effectively new capacity without new grid connections.
insights.quote: Every unused watt is capacity left on the table.

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims DSX MaxLPS policy-governed power sharing lets customers deploy up to 40% more GPUs within the same approved power budget.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: If broadly realized, up to 40% more GPUs per power envelope raises GPU demand per MW of data-center capacity.
insights.quote: enabling customers to deploy up to 40% more GPUs within the same approved power budget

insights.claim: Because training cycles through compute, communication, synchronization and checkpointing, and inference alternates prefill, decode, memory-bound, network and idle phases, AI workloads rarely draw constant power, creating a gap between reserved peak and actual consumption.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Workload power variability is the economic basis for oversubscription, similar to how cloud providers oversubscribe CPUs.
insights.quote: AI workloads rarely draw constant power

insights.claim: With static per-node power reservations, unused power in one node cannot be shifted to another, so a facility can sit below its aggregate limit while extra GPU capacity stays offline.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Explains why power-constrained operators can grow token output via software rather than waiting for utility upgrades.
insights.quote: The aggregate facility can remain below its limit while additional GPU capacity stays offline.

insights.claim: MaxLPS is coordinated allocation beneath the existing managed budget, not an increase in the site's power supply.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Gains come from utilization, not new energy, which matters for sites blocked on interconnect queues.
insights.quote: This is coordinated allocation, not an increase in the site’s power supply.

insights.claim: DSX MaxLPS optimizes AI factory output within land, power and shell (LPS) constraints, with NVIDIA Dynamic Power Software as the control layer for policy-governed allocation.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is monetizing facility-level software that ties data-center power management to its hardware stack.
insights.locator: Inside the DSX MaxLPS control loop

insights.claim: The control process has five elements: topology and resource groups with an aggregate budget, multi-level power telemetry, operator policy (limits, priorities, reserves, emergency responses), dynamic GPU power-limit allocation, and validation/enforcement against the group budget.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Provides a checklist for evaluating competing power-orchestration products.
insights.locator: The control process has five technical elements

themes.theme: Measured results from the Nscale evaluation

insights.claim: The NVIDIA-Nscale evaluation ran Kimi K2.5 in FP4 on GB300 NVL72 (Blackwell Ultra) systems with NVIDIA Dynamo and TensorRT LLM at Nscale's renewable-powered Verne campus in Keflavík, Iceland, using 8K input and 1K output sequences.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Real-world validation with a neocloud operator (Nscale) using a Chinese open-weight model on NVIDIA's latest shipping rack.

insights.claim: The static baseline ran 140 GPUs (35 four-GPU nodes) while the MaxLPS configuration ran 192 GPUs (48 nodes), a 37.1% increase, under the same 264.4 kW provisioned power budget.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Quantifies roughly 37% more GPU density per provisioned kW in a real deployment.
insights.quote: Both configurations used the same 264.4 kW provisioned power budget.

insights.claim: Aggregate throughput rose 49.2% from 1,084,503 to 1,618,443 tokens/s, and throughput per provisioned watt rose from 4.10 to 6.12 tokens/s/W.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Token output per provisioned watt is the key revenue metric for power-limited AI factories; ~49% uplift materially improves unit economics.
insights.quote: The baseline delivered 4.10 tokens/s/W, and DSX MaxLPS delivered 6.12 tokens/s/W, a 49.2% increase.

insights.claim: Per-instance throughput was essentially unchanged (high-throughput 59,153 vs 59,220 tokens/s; low-latency 2,265 vs 2,265 tokens/s), meaning the added fleet did not degrade existing instances' throughput.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Suggests the extra capacity is nearly free in throughput terms for existing tenants.

insights.claim: Total measured power rose only 19.7% (166.2 kW to 198.9 kW) and power-budget utilization went from 62.9% to 75.2%, showing the baseline used well under two-thirds of its provisioned budget.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Even with MaxLPS roughly a quarter of provisioned power remained unused, implying further headroom in conventionally provisioned AI sites.

insights.claim: Throughput grew 49.2% while GPU count grew only 37.1%, because the added capacity was a third high-throughput instance while the low-latency instance was held constant.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Headline gains depend on the workload mix added, so investors should not extrapolate 49% uniformly.
insights.locator: The static baseline used 35 four-GPU nodes

insights.claim: Median and P75 latency stayed within 5% of baseline, but P99 time to first token rose 17% from a 15.7-second baseline.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Tail latency degradation may limit oversubscription for latency-sensitive, SLA-bound inference services.
insights.quote: P99 time to first token increased 17% from the 15.7-second baseline

insights.claim: Dynamic power allocation makes engineering trade-offs observable and controllable at fleet level but does not eliminate them.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Tempers vendor claims: gains come with service-quality costs operators must price in.
insights.quote: Dynamic power allocation makes engineering trade-offs observable and controllable at the fleet level; it does not eliminate them.

insights.claim: Available headroom depends on workload mix: complementary power profiles create more opportunity than workloads that peak simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Homogeneous training clusters may see smaller gains than heterogeneous inference fleets.
insights.quote: complementary power profiles create more opportunity than workloads that peak simultaneously
insights.locator: DSX MaxLPS uses previously unused headroom

insights.claim: Dynamic allocation depends on reliable telemetry, and missing, delayed or mis-mapped measurements can undermine fleet-level decisions.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Creates demand for power metering and telemetry infrastructure as a prerequisite for oversubscription.
insights.quote: Missing, delayed, or incorrectly mapped measurements can undermine fleet-level decisions.
insights.locator: Dynamic allocation depends on reliable telemetry

insights.claim: NVIDIA recommends a five-stage validation: define the managed boundary, establish a representative baseline, introduce policies conservatively, add capacity incrementally with testing, and set production operating limits only when all objectives are met.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Adoption will be gradual and operator-driven, so revenue/capacity uplift will phase in rather than arrive at once.
insights.locator: How operators can validate DSX MaxLPS

insights.claim: Sites should size electrical distribution, cooling, network fabric, floor space and rack positions for the validated lifecycle target even if fewer racks are populated on day one.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Implies higher upfront spend on non-power infrastructure per MW, benefiting cooling, networking and rack suppliers.
insights.quote: the site must be able to host the capacity it enables
insights.locator: Plan the site for the validated

insights.claim: For future Vera Rubin NVL72 AI factories, DSX MaxLPS will combine dynamic power management with performance-per-watt techniques and infrastructure designed for 45°C liquid-cooling inlet operation, though NVIDIA says any Vera Rubin projection should be kept separate from the measured GB300 results.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: 45°C inlet liquid cooling points to warm-water cooling designs that reduce chiller needs in next-gen deployments.
insights.quote: infrastructure designed for 45°C liquid-cooling inlet operation
insights.locator: For future NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72
